content: Periodontal disease and dental caries are common oral health issues that can cause pain, discomfort, aesthetic concerns, and eventually tooth loss. These conditions are expensive to treat and place a significant burden on healthcare systems. Triclosan is an antibacterial agent with low toxicity that, when combined with a copolymer to enhance retention, can be incorporated into toothpastes to reduce plaque and gingivitis. It is essential that these additional ingredients do not interfere with the fluoride's anticaries effects in toothpaste and that they are safe for use. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of fluoride toothpastes containing triclosan/copolymer compared to fluoride toothpastes without triclosan/copolymer for the long-term management of caries, plaque, and gingivitis in both children and adults. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed the impact of triclosan/copolymer-containing toothpastes on oral health. A total of 30 studies involving 14,835 participants were included. Of these, 10 studies were assessed as having a low risk of bias, 9 as having a high risk of bias, and 11 as having an unclear risk of bias. Plaque: After six to seven months of use, triclosan/copolymer toothpaste reduced plaque levels by 0.47 on a 0 to 5 scale (mean difference [MD] -0.47, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.60 to -0.34, 20 studies, 2675 participants, moderate-quality evidence). The control group had a mean plaque score of 2.17, indicating a 22% reduction in plaque. Additionally, the proportion of sites scoring 3 to 5 on the plaque scale was reduced by 0.15 (MD -0.15, 95% CI -0.20 to -0.10, 13 studies, 1850 participants, moderate-quality evidence), representing a 41% reduction in plaque severity. Gingivitis: After six to nine months of use, triclosan/copolymer toothpaste reduced gingival inflammation by 0.27 on a 0 to 3 scale (MD -0.27, 95% CI -0.33 to -0.21, 20 studies, 2743 participants, moderate-quality evidence). The control group had a mean inflammation score of 1.22, representing a 22% reduction in inflammation. Furthermore, the proportion of bleeding sites (scoring 2 or 3 on the 0 to 3 scale) was reduced by 0.13 (MD -0.13, 95% CI -0.17 to -0.08, 15 studies, 1998 participants, moderate-quality evidence), indicating a 48% reduction in gingival bleeding. Periodontitis: After 36 months of use, there was no evidence of a difference between triclosan/copolymer toothpaste and control toothpaste in the prevention of periodontitis, as measured by attachment loss (risk ratio [RR] 0.92, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.27, one study, 480 participants, low-quality evidence). Caries: After 24 to 36 months of use, triclosan/copolymer toothpaste slightly reduced coronal caries, as measured by the decayed and filled surfaces (DFS) index (MD -0.16, 95% CI -0.31 to -0.02, four studies, 9692 participants, high-quality evidence). The control group had a mean DFS score of 3.44, representing a 5% reduction in coronal caries. Additionally, after 36 months of use, triclosan/copolymer toothpaste probably reduced root caries (MD -0.31, 95% CI -0.39 to -0.23, one study, 1357 participants, moderate-quality evidence). Calculus: After six months of use, triclosan/copolymer toothpaste may have reduced the mean total calculus per participant by 2.12 mm (MD -2.12 mm, 95% CI -3.39 to -0.84, two studies, 415 participants, low-quality evidence). The control group had a mean calculus score of 14.61 mm, representing a 15% reduction in calculus. Adverse Effects: There were no data available for meta-analysis regarding adverse effects. However, 22 studies (73%) reported no adverse effects associated with either the experimental or control toothpaste. Heterogeneity: There was considerable heterogeneity in the meta-analyses for plaque, gingivitis, and calculus. Despite this, the results for plaque and gingivitis were consistent enough to support the conclusions, though readers are advised to interpret the findings with caution. Conclusions: Moderate-quality evidence indicates that toothpastes containing triclosan/copolymer, in addition to fluoride, reduce plaque, gingival inflammation, and gingival bleeding compared to fluoride toothpastes without triclosan/copolymer. These reductions may or may not be clinically significant and are observed regardless of initial plaque and gingivitis levels or whether a baseline oral prophylaxis was performed. High-quality evidence shows that triclosan/copolymer toothpastes lead to a small reduction in coronal caries. There is weaker evidence suggesting that these toothpastes may reduce root caries and calculus, but there is insufficient evidence to determine their effect on preventing periodontitis. No serious safety concerns were identified in studies lasting up to three years.
